RIGHTS

Common law rights: The traditional status of rights in the UK has been that every citizen was assumed to have rights unless they were prohibited by law. ‘Negative rights’. Rights were also sometimes specifically stated as a result of a court case when these rights were in dispute, in doing so a judge was declaring Common Law. This creates judicial precedent.

HRA 1998: The HRA brought into effect the ECHR, which was established by the Council of Europe in 1950. The UK helped to draft the Convention but did not accept it as binding on its government until 1998.
Traditionally, the UK relied on a series of negative rights, meaning they existed in an absence of law and were very difficult to enforce, with people’s protections very limited.
With the introduction of the HRA, these negative rights were supplanted by positive rights that had to be legally protected and respected.
HRA is binding on all public bodies other than the UK parliament (politically binding but not legally binding) and enforced by all courts in the UK
Freedom of Information Act 2000: Historically, citizens had no right to see information held by public bodies. Labour gov of 1997 thus passed this Act.

Has proved an invaluable tool for social and political campaigners, for MPs and for the media, allowing them to discover information that was never available in the past. Helped to improve services such as the health service, the police, the civil service and educational establishments by shedding light on their activities.
It was through the Freedom of Information Act that the Daily Telegraph was able to publicised the MPs expenses scandal of 2009

The Equality Act 2010: the two parliamentary statutes prior to the Equality Act that established formal equality in the UK (The Race Relations Act 1965 and The Equal Pay act 1970) missed out many important groups in society who have suffered discrimination)
The Act requires that all legislation and decision-making made by government at any level must take into account formal equality of different sections of society.

1979 GENERAL ELECTION

Labour government, which had come to power with a small majority in 1974 had suffered the loss of a number of MPs and repeated crises. By 1979, public opinion had turned against labour, allowing the conservatives, under Margaret Thatcher, to make large gains and win a clear majority
Conservatives were to be in power for the next 18 years
Conservatives: 63 more seats than previous election, 43.9% of the vote, 43 seat majority
Labour: 50 fewer seats than previous election, 36.9% of the vote
Demographic:
Sharp decline in number of people describing themselves as ‘working class’ at the time of this election. May have eroded Labour’s vote.
Conversely, the middle class was growing, helping the conservatives
Key issue: power of trade unions and economy
‘Winter of Discontent’: Winter of 1978-1979 there had been a wave of strikes by public-sector workers, leading to bins being left unemptied, shortages of power and disruption of public transport
Which party was best placed to control union power?
UK economy saw high inflation, growing unemployment and falling growth. Conservative response was to plan a return to free markets and to curb union power
They argued that prices would come down if unemployment continued to rise so that wages would fall
Party leaders
James Callaghan, Labour PM before the election, ironically had a more favourable image than Thatcher
Seen as reliable and likeable where Thatcher was seen as distant and too ‘posh’
Thatcher had also been unpopular as education secretary in the early 1970s
Some members of the electorate may have been reluctant to vote for a female PM
Conservatives thus won in spite of rather than because of their leader
Turnout
Turnout was a little down on past trends, largely due to abstentions by the working class and union members, who were labour’s core voters
Opinion polls may have played a role in boosting Conservative turn-it as they showed an increasingly close race
Campaign
1979 election was the first campaign where the parties focused on using the media, rather than having the media passively report on what had happened without sharing opinions

Press conferences were timed to provide stories for the midday news, afternoon walkabouts by leaders were designed to coincide with the early evening news, and major speeches were timed to make the late evening news

As a result of opinion polls, which showed that the public did not like adversarial campaigns, the two main parties avoided making attacks on each other, especially after criticism was levelled at the conservatives following an insult-laden first ‘attack and’
While Callaghan certainly ‘won’ the campaign, coming across as the more popular leader and closing the polling gap between labour and the conservatives, it was not enough to win the election
1997 GENERAL ELECTION

In 1992, the conservatives had won a fourth election in a row with a majority of 23 seats. Since then. Their reputation as a party of government had suffered and the Labour Party had reformed as ‘New Labour’ under Tony Blair. The 1997 election resulted in the Tory Party’s worst electoral defeat since 1906 and Labour’s largest ever electoral victory
Massive defeat for conservatives which took them over 10 years to recover, Labour stayed in power for next 13 years
Labour: 145 more seats than previous election, 43.2% of vote, 179 seat majority
Conservative: 165 fewer seats than previous election, 30.7% of the vote,
Demographic:
Blair and Labour leadership recognised that the traditional working class, Labour’s natural core vote, was diminishing in size and the party couldn’t rely on it to get into power
Therefore decided to ‘woo’ the middle classes, part of the conservatives’ core vote, by adopting centrist policies
Young were also persuaded to vote Labour as it represented a break from traditional, out-of-date politics
Valence:
Image of Tory party, which had been in power for 18 years, was tired, and the party was divided over Europe
Tories had also presided over a deep economic recession in the early 1990s – competence
Labour had no economic record to defend and appeared to be a younger, fresher party, united around a definable set of policies – the ‘third way’
The main problem for Tories was that the electorate remembered the recession of the late 80s and early 90s and blamed the party for it. General sense that the conservatives mismanaged the economy
Party leaders
Conservative Prime Minister John Major appeared grey, unexciting and weak whereas Tony Blair was clearly in command, young and attractive, with a clear vision
Liberal Democrat leader, Paddy Ashdown, had a positive image which led to 30 seat increase for Lib Dem’s from previous election
Turnout

Beginning of long-term decline in turnout, a watershed in political participation
Political issues: NHS/ Education and party image

Chancellor Gordon Brown promised to be financially responsible, which was a strong message, especially as Labour had a bad reputation as a ‘tax and spend’ party
Labour was fortunate that economic recovery was under way when it took office, so it could pay for the improvements in public services

In the years 1992-94 John Major had presided over Conservative Party divided over the Maastricht treaty, which transferred huge amounts of power to the EU, hangover from this still present in 1997, as was the party’s reputation for ‘sleaze’
Campaign
Election campaign lasted 6 weeks, far longer than 31 day average previously
Major hoped this would expose labour divisions and put pressure on Blair
Both campaigns focused on the leaders, touring marginal seats and using campaign buses and planes
Labours campaign was strict and well organised, run from the Millbank Media Centre
Use of media soundbites, like Blair’s three priorities being ‘education, education, education’ helped galvanise the public
Conservatives focused on fears of Labour restoring union power and Blair being untrustworthy
Conservative Party had to spend much of its time dealing with the issue of sleaze and financial corruption, which distracted from its wider campaign
Conservatives tried to focus on negative anti-labour campaign while Labour focused on positive ‘pro-Blair’ campaign
Elections saw enormous step towards disciplined, media-focused electioneering modelled on US politics
Policies
Conservatives tried to focus policies on economic recovery, but the issue of Europe dominated and divided the party, especially with the presence of the Referendum Party

Labour focused on five specific pledges: cut class sizes in schools, introduce fast track punishment for young offenders, cut NHS waiting lists, get 250,000 unemployed under 15s into work, cut VAT and not raise income tax

Much more accurate in 1997, but the legacy of distrust from 1992 meant that New Labour did not believe them and kept campaigning as if they might lose
By showing Labour as clear favourite, turnout might have been suppressed slightly

Following the close election and minority government of 2017, both main parties had seen divisions grow. Demographic issues:

Shift in working class support across northern industrial areas as former labour and UKIP voters - tired of the Brexit deadlock, voted for the conservatives over Labour, reducing the ‘red wall’ of northern support
Labour continued to focus on younger and working-class voters with more socialist manifesto
Conservatives focused on appealing to older and working class voters angry over the failure to deliver Brexit
Valence and Brexit
Parliament had been in chaos since the previous election and the public had been frustrated by all sides’ inability to move forward on Brexit
Consequently, the clear message being offered by new PM Boris Johnson on Brexit became the main focus of the campaign, compared with the vague and complicated messages of the Labour Party

The issue of antisemitism dominated the Labour Party in the run-up to the election, as did the formation of new parties, including Nigel Farage’s Brexit Party and the creation of the Independent Group for Change

The decision of the Brexit party not to contest seats won by the Conservatives in 2010 and seats with strong Conservative Brexit supporters meant the right predominantly only had one party to choose on the issue

Liberal Democrat had seen their total number of MPs increase to 21 with defections from both Labour and the Conservatives, but this only seemed to alienate supporters who did not want to be associated with members of one of the main parties

Boris Johnson benefited from having been PM and leader for a limited time and stuck to a strategy of not appearing too often in the media, instead relying on his existing reputation and media profile from his time as London Mayor

summary: Labour government, which had come to power with a small majority in 1974 had suffered the loss of a number of MPs and repeated crises. By 1979, public opinion had turned against labour, allowing the conservatives, under Margaret Thatcher, to make large gains and win a clear majority
Conservatives were to be in power for the next 18 years
results: Conservatives: 63 more seats than previous election, 43.9% of the vote, 43 seat majority
Labour: 50 fewer seats than previous election, 36.9% of the vote

Demographic: Sharp decline in number of people describing themselves as ‘working class’ at the time of this election. May have eroded Labour’s vote.
Conversely, the middle class was growing, helping the conservatives
Key issue: ‘Winter of Discontent’: Winter of 1978-1979 there had been a wave of strikes by public-sector workers, leading to bins being left unemptied, shortages of power and disruption of public transport
Which party was best placed to control union power?
UK economy saw high inflation, growing unemployment and falling growth. Conservative response was to plan a return to free markets and to curb union power
They argued that prices would come down if unemployment continued to rise so that wages would fall
Party leaders: James Callaghan, Labour PM before the election, ironically had a more favourable image than Thatcher
Seen as reliable and likeable where Thatcher was seen as distant and too ‘posh’
Thatcher had also been unpopular as education secretary in the early 1970s
Some members of the electorate may have been reluctant to vote for a female PM
Conservatives thus won in spite of rather than because of their leader
Turnout: Turnout was a little down on past trends, largely due to abstentions by the working class and union members, who were labour’s core voters
Opinion polls may have played a role in boosting Conservative turn-it as they showed an increasingly close race
Campaign: 1979 election was the first campaign where the parties focused on using the media, rather than having the media passively report on what had happened without sharing opinions

Press conferences were timed to provide stories for the midday news, afternoon walkabouts by leaders were designed to coincide with the early evening news, and major speeches were timed to make the late evening news

As a result of opinion polls, which showed that the public did not like adversarial campaigns, the two main parties avoided making attacks on each other, especially after criticism was levelled at the conservatives following an insult-laden first ‘attack and’
While Callaghan certainly ‘won’ the campaign, coming across as the more popular leader and closing the polling gap between labour and the conservatives, it was not enough to win the election

summary: In 1992, the conservatives had won a fourth election in a row with a majority of 23 seats. Since then. Their reputation as a party of government had suffered and the Labour Party had reformed as ‘New Labour’ under Tony Blair. The 1997 election resulted in the Tory Party’s worst electoral defeat since 1906 and Labour’s largest ever electoral victory
Massive defeat for conservatives which took them over 10 years to recover, Labour stayed in power for next 13 years
results: Labour: 145 more seats than previous election, 43.2% of vote, 179 seat majority
Conservative: 165 fewer seats than previous election, 30.7% of the vote,

Demographic: Blair and Labour leadership recognised that the traditional working class, Labour’s natural core vote, was diminishing in size and the party couldn’t rely on it to get into power
Therefore decided to ‘woo’ the middle classes, part of the conservatives’ core vote, by adopting centrist policies
Young were also persuaded to vote Labour as it represented a break from traditional, out-of-date politics
Valence: Image of Tory party, which had been in power for 18 years, was tired, and the party was divided over Europe
Tories had also presided over a deep economic recession in the early 1990s – competence
Labour had no economic record to defend and appeared to be a younger, fresher party, united around a definable set of policies – the ‘third way’
The main problem for Tories was that the electorate remembered the recession of the late 80s and early 90s and blamed the party for it. General sense that the conservatives mismanaged the economy
Party leaders: Conservative Prime Minister John Major appeared grey, unexciting and weak whereas Tony Blair was clearly in command, young and attractive, with a clear vision
Liberal Democrat leader, Paddy Ashdown, had a positive image which led to 30 seat increase for Lib Dem’s from previous election
Turnout: Figure of 71% seems healthy by moderns tankards but was much lower than typical levels in the past
Beginning of long-term decline in turnout, a watershed in political participation
Political issues: Both services had been in decline, Labour promised to make huge investments in both in order to raise standards
Chancellor Gordon Brown promised to be financially responsible, which was a strong message, especially as Labour had a bad reputation as a ‘tax and spend’ party
Labour was fortunate that economic recovery was under way when it took office, so it could pay for the improvements in public services

In the years 1992-94 John Major had presided over Conservative Party divided over the Maastricht treaty, which transferred huge amounts of power to the EU, hangover from this still present in 1997, as was the party’s reputation for ‘sleaze’
Campaign: Election campaign lasted 6 weeks, far longer than 31 day average previously
Major hoped this would expose labour divisions and put pressure on Blair
Both campaigns focused on the leaders, touring marginal seats and using campaign buses and planes
Labours campaign was strict and well organised, run from the Millbank Media Centre
Use of media soundbites, like Blair’s three priorities being ‘education, education, education’ helped galvanise the public
Conservatives focused on fears of Labour restoring union power and Blair being untrustworthy
Conservative Party had to spend much of its time dealing with the issue of sleaze and financial corruption, which distracted from its wider campaign
Conservatives tried to focus on negative anti-labour campaign while Labour focused on positive ‘pro-Blair’ campaign
Elections saw enormous step towards disciplined, media-focused electioneering modelled on US politics
Policies: Conservatives tried to focus policies on economic recovery, but the issue of Europe dominated and divided the party, especially with the presence of the Referendum Party

Labour focused on five specific pledges: cut class sizes in schools, introduce fast track punishment for young offenders, cut NHS waiting lists, get 250,000 unemployed under 15s into work, cut VAT and not raise income tax
Opinion polls: Having been spectacularly wrong in 1992, the polls made a more concerted effort to survey a wider cross-section of society
Much more accurate in 1997, but the legacy of distrust from 1992 meant that New Labour did not believe them and kept campaigning as if they might lose
By showing Labour as clear favourite, turnout might have been suppressed slightly

summary: 2010 UK saw the creation of its first coalition government since WW2. Lib Dem’s paid the price and were almost wiped out as a parliamentary party, losing seats across England, mostly to the Conservative Party. The SNP broke Labour’s traditional dominance of Scotland and replaced the Lib Dem’s as the third party in Westminster. Conservatives won their first majority since 1992.
Shock of defeat completely destabilised Labour Party
Huge left-wing backlash over failed policies of the leadership, leading to the party electing extreme left-winger Jeremy Corbyn in place of Ed Milliband
results: Conservatives: 28 more seats than 2010, 36.9% of the vote, 12 seat majority
Labour: 24 fewer seats than 2010, 30.4% of vote
Lib Dem: 48 fewer seats than 2010, 8 seats

Demographic: Large proportion of Labour’s core working-class vote was captured by UKIP, especially in depressed areas of the country
Lib Dem’s lost all 15 of their seats in southwest England. Dispelled the idea that they had a core vote in that region
Conservatives dominated south of England as a whole
SNP nearly swept the board in Scotland, Labour’s regional heartland taken away
Valence: All parties suffered from negative image other than SNP
Conservatives still divided over Europe and immigration
Lib Dem’s blamed for many of the shortcomings of the previous coalition government
Labour not trusted with the economy and its competence was constantly called into question
Media may have had an impact of warning about the dangers of a likely Labour-SNP coalition, as indicated by opinion polls – some voters turned away from this prospect by voting for conservatives
UKIP took more votes from Labour than conservatives
Conservatives benefitted from collapse of Lib Dem voting.
Party leaders: All leaders other than SNP Nicola Sturgeon suffered a negative image
David Cameron’s image was the least negative
Nick Clegg of Lib Dem and Ed Milliband of Labour were both short of public respect
Political issues: Conservatives still more trusted with the economy than Labour
Election was dominated by the prospect of a referendum on UK membership of the EU
Conservatives and UKIP were rewarded fir their support of such a referendum
Scottish referendum of 2014 was a key event, put the SNP in a powerful position in Scotland
Campaigns: Second campaign in which televised debates featured
Cameron refused to debate with Milliband head-to-head, agreeing only to a seven-person leadership debate, which proved bland and made it difficult for Milliband to stand out
Although Labour focused on the NHS and many celebrity endorsements, Conservatives focused on working families and questioned ‘Labour’s magic money tree’ which was more effective
Both sides stressed the dangers of possible coalition, either SNP-Labour or Conservative-UKIP
Conservatives focused heavily on campaigning agains the Lib Dem’s in England as a means of preventing Labour-SNP coalition
SNP targeted both Labour and Lib Dems for failing to consider Scottish issues
Policies: Labour focused on five key pledges: To balance the books and cut the deficit, to freeze energy bills until 2017, to recruit 20,000 more nurses and 8000 more GPs, to prevent Immigrants claiming benefits for 2 years, to reduce uni tuition fees to 6000 per year

Conservatives pledged to make welfare cuts, but refused to say where these cuts would be until after the election. Promised in/out EU referendum, tax-free income for those on minimum wage, up to 20 hours per week of free childcare
Opinion polls: Increasingly reliant on digital methods, got it wrong by underestimating the number of older voters who would turnout and be more likely to vote Tory
Labour thus chose to fight a campaign on Labour policies rather than anti-conservative
Labour-SNP threats may have influenced tactical voting and boosted Conservative turnout

summary: Following the close election and minority government of 2017, both main parties had seen divisions grow. It was not clear how the 2019 election would play out, but Labour’s vote collapsed across the UK, allowing the conservative’s to win their largest majority since the 1987 election. In Scotland, the SNP made significant gains, having fallen back in 2017.

Conservatives were given a clear mandate and ensured continued dominance of the Conservative Party since 2010. First sizeable majority since the 2005 election and saw Jeremy Corbyn resign as Labour leader.
results: Conservatives, 47 more seats, 43.6% of vote, 80 seat majority

Demographic: Shift in working class support across northern industrial areas as former labour and UKIP voters - tired of the Brexit deadlock, voted for the conservatives over Labour, reducing the ‘red wall’ of northern support
Labour continued to focus on younger and working-class voters with more socialist manifesto
Conservatives focused on appealing to older and working class voters angry over the failure to deliver Brexit
Valence: Parliament had been in chaos since the previous election and the public had been frustrated by all sides’ inability to move forward on Brexit
Consequently, the clear message being offered by new PM Boris Johnson on Brexit became the main focus of the campaign, compared with the vague and complicated messages of the Labour Party

The issue of antisemitism dominated the Labour Party in the run-up to the election, as did the formation of new parties, including Nigel Farage’s Brexit Party and the creation of the Independent Group for Change

The decision of the Brexit party not to contest seats won by the Conservatives in 2010 and seats with strong Conservative Brexit supporters meant the right predominantly only had one party to choose on the issue

Liberal Democrat had seen their total number of MPs increase to 21 with defections from both Labour and the Conservatives, but this only seemed to alienate supporters who did not want to be associated with members of one of the main parties
Issue of Scottish independence saw the SNP gain more seats
Party leaders: Boris Johnson benefited from having been PM and leader for a limited time and stuck to a strategy of not appearing too often in the media, instead relying on his existing reputation and media profile from his time as London Mayor
Unlike Theresa May in 2017, he appeared focused and more determined and clear in his policy-making than Jeremy Corbyn
Nicola Sturgeon continued to enjoy a positive image in Scotland
Liberal Democrat leader Jo Swanson alienated the public by appearing to lack sincerity and pledging to repeal Article 50
Turnout: Turnout saw a slight drop in 2019 from the 69% of 2017, perhaps because this was a less close election than previously but also perhaps because a December election encouraged some voters
Campaign: Campaign was more subdued than previous ones partly because it took place during the winter and partly because Johnson seemed to be absent for much of the campaign, appearing in public relatively rarely for a serving leader
Although he did participate in a head-to-head debate with Corbyn, the main objective seemed to be to let the issue of Brexit persuade the voters
The slogan ‘Get Brexit Done’, coined by Dominic Cummings, was particularly influential
Corbyn managed a solid campaign with lots of public speeches but was unable to whip up the enthusiasm he had in 2017
Social media attack ads were more prevent in this campaign than in any other and the Electoral commission seemed unable to do much about it
Political issues/ rational choice
The election cycle was dominated by the extension of the deadline for leaving the EU from October 2019 to January 2020 and the inability of parliament to find a solution for Brexit
Former big names from both main parties urged members not to vote for their party, including Michael Heseltine and John Major on the Conservative side and Alistair Campbell for Labour
During the Campaign, floods hit parts of England and Johnson was criticised for not declaring them an emergency
Journalists from the Labour-supporting Mirror newspaper were banned from the Conservative campaign bus
Shortly before the election, a NATO summit was held in Watford, allowing Johnson to appear with other world leaders, including President Donald Trump
Opinion polls: Opinion polls were again under scrutiny with the memory of 2015
The polls seemed to indicate a conservative win throughout, which perhaps shaped the campaign as one for the conservatives to lose rather than for Labour to win
The polls underestimated the scale of conservative victory

Liberty: National Council for Civil Liberties (NCCL)
Non-profit, operates like a think tank and membership association, causal pressure group

Its objectives are to fight to protect and uphold civil rights and liberties across the UK and to develop a wider ‘rights culture’ across society
Methods

Uses both mainstream traditional media and social media to spread awareness and develop support
Supports and brings legal challenges against rights abuses, challenging what it regards as unfair or unjust laws that restrict civil liberties - E.g recent legal challenge to lockdown restrictions

Traditionally done through a letter-writing campaign – local branches and smaller groups tasked with writing to an ‘at-risk individual’ to show support as well as writing letters to the government concerned or to other governments in the hope that they will pressurise the offending government into taking action

Gives advice and produces template letters and emails for people to fill in themselves

concepts.definition: The traditional status of rights in the UK has been that every citizen was assumed to have rights unless they were prohibited by law. ‘Negative rights’. Rights were also sometimes specifically stated as a result of a court case when these rights were in dispute, in doing so a judge was declaring Common Law. This creates judicial precedent.
The HRA brought into effect the ECHR, which was established by the Council of Europe in 1950. The UK helped to draft the Convention but did not accept it as binding on its government until 1998.
extras: Traditionally, the UK relied on a series of negative rights, meaning they existed in an absence of law and were very difficult to enforce, with people’s protections very limited.
With the introduction of the HRA, these negative rights were supplanted by positive rights that had to be legally protected and respected.
HRA is binding on all public bodies other than the UK parliament (politically binding but not legally binding) and enforced by all courts in the UK

tables.label: Direct vs Representative Democracy
rows:
Purest form of democracy. The people’s voice is clearly heard 
It can avoid delay and deadlock within a political system
The fact that the people are making the decision gives it great legitimacy 
 
Referendums have higher turnout than general elections, with 2024 GE having 60% (second lowest since universal suffrage) and 2014 independence (84%) 2016 Brexit (72%)

It can lead to the ‘tyranny of the majority’ whereby the winning majority simply ignores the interests of the minority and imposes something detrimental on them 
The people may be too easily swayed by short-term, emotional appeals by charismatic individuals 
Some issues may be too complex for the ordinary citizen to understand 

Misinformation during 2016 Brexit referendum, misleading bus claim ‘We send the EU 350 million a week, lets fund our NHS instead’

tables.label: Direct vs Representative Democracy (alt view)
rows:
Representatives can develop expertise to deal with matters the public does not have the time or knowledge to deal with 
Representatives can be held to account for their actions at election time 
Representatives have the time to deal with a variety of complex matters, leaving the public free to get on with their own lives
In a large modern country, it is the only practical way to translate public opinion into political action
Elected representatives may have better judgement and be more rational/ not swayed by emotion 
Representatives can protect the interests of minority groups 

Reform UK MP for Great Yarmouth, Rupert Lowe, voted in favour of the landmark Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill 2024 after hosting a mini-referendum in his constituency, 75% yes 

December 5 2023, 22 Conservative MPs supported a Labour amendment aimed at speeding up compensation for victims of the infected blood scandal, rebelling against a 3 line conservative whip to do so

Representatives may not act in the best interests of their constituents 
It can be difficult to hold a representative to account between elections 
Allowing voters to delegate responsibility to representatives can lead to the public disengaging from social issues and other responsibilities 
Representative bodies can be unrepresentative and may ignore the concerns and needs of minority groups 

FPTP leads to votes of unequal value, marginal seats have votes that matter more, e.g Thanet South, Kent which has been won by the winning party at every GE since its creation 

Economist reported in December 2024 that since 2010, former MPs and ministers have spent a total of 50,000 hours an earned 65 million from doing second jobs 

YouGov polling, 49% of respondents say they ‘almost never’ trust the British government to place the needs of the nation above the interests of their own party

Rise of new groups around environmental issues since 60s, people feel that single issue groups are more effective than parties

2024 consistent protests in London and across UK for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza

tables.label: How democratic is the UK system?
rows: Peaceful transition of power
The uk is remarkably conflict-free
Short-lived disputes have arisen when the results were not clear, in 2010 and in 2017, leading to some claims of a lack of legitimacy
Free elections

Nearly everyone over 18 can vote 
There is little electoral fraud and there exist strong legal safeguards

Some groups, such as prisoners and effectively the homeless, are denied their right to vote and new voter ID laws are believed to have added to the disenfranchised 
The HOL is not elected, nor is the head of state (monarch)
Fair elections
There are proportional systems in place in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland and other devolved and local bodies

The FPTP system for general elections leads to disproportionate results and many wasted votes 
Governments are often elected on a modest proportion of the popular vote
Widespread participation
There is extensive membership of pressure groups, which are free and active. There is also a growing level of participation in e-democracy

Since 2001, voter turnout in general elections has been, on average, lower than in previous elections, while party membership, especially among the young, has generally been in decline. 
Despite some increases in party membership after 2015, it is still below levels experienced in the 1950s
Freedom of expression
The press and broadcast media are free of government interference. Broadcast media maintain political neutrality. There is free access to the internet

Much ownership of the press is in the hands of a few large, powerful companies such as News international, the owners of which tend to have their own political preferences 
Some information available on the internet is false and detrimental 
There is some dependent over how independent the BBC is and attempts by politicians to influence its reporting
Freedom of association

There are no restrictions on legal organisations 
People may organise and instigate public protests

The government has the power to ban some groups based on the potentially unfair perception of their activities 
Public meetings and demonstrations can be restricted on the grounds of ‘public order’
Protection of rights and liberties

The country is singed up to the ECHR 
The HOL advocates for rights

Parliament is sovereign, which means rights are at the mercy of a government with a strong majority in the commons 
The ECHR is not binding on the UK parliament
The rule of law

Upheld strictly by the judiciary 
The right to judicial review underpins this 
The judiciary is independent and non-political

The monarch is exempt from legal restrictions 
There is statistical evidence to suggest social and economic standing impact severity of sentencing
A constitution

Parliament and the courts ensure the government acts within the law 
The HRA acts as a restraint on the actions of the gov, and constitutional checks exist to limit the power of gov

There is no codified UK constitution so the limits on government power are vague 
Parliamentary sovereignty means the government’s power could be increased without a constitutional safeguard 
The prerogative powers of the PM are extensive and arbitrary

tables.label: Factors influencing pressure group success
rows: Size of membership

The more supporters a group has, the more pressure It can place on decision-makers 
Politicians do not like to fly in the face of public opinion because they regularly face the need of re-election
Smaller groups can be overlooked or ‘drowned out’ by the campaigns of larger groups. They find it harder to raise funds and achieve their goals with fewer participants
Finance
Wealthy groups can afford expensive campaigns, employ lobbyists, sponsor political parties and purchase favourable publicity
Groups with less funding struggle to organise effective campaigns, hire lobbyists and fund production of leaflets, websites and other research, and therefore struggle to make their voices heard
The strategic position of a particular sectional group

A group that Is seen as more important to the economy or a key service cam put greater pressure on the government 
Companies and industrial groups have a great deal of leverage because they are vital to the economy, as do NHS workers

Groups that are not seen as important can easily be ignored, especially if they are competing against a strategically important group: the Occupy movement failed in part because it was up against the strategically important finance sector
Public mood
The combination of public sentiment and strong campaigning can be successful in bringing an issue to the attention of decision-makers as politicians are more likely to support a popular cause
Public mood can turn politicians against certain groups, either for the issue they champion, such as prisoner or terrorist rights, or because the methods they use alienate public opinion
Attitude of the government
Groups are far more likely to achieve success if the government of the day is sympathetic to their cause and position

If the government of the day is determined to follow a particular course of action that a group opposes, it is very unlikely that they will be able to change the government’s decision, notably seen in the failure of the 2003 Stop the War coalition

rows:

Parliament has previously changed decisions based on the rulings of the European Courts e.g Parliament formation of the Modern Slavery Act 2015, Case brought which criticised UK for not having robust laws against forced labour and domestic servitude 
Mental Capacity Act 2005 which passed following a ruling in the ECHR which found that the UK lacked adequate legal protection for the liberty of people with mental capacity issues who were detained

January 2026 Reform UK’s Farage and Conservatives Badenoch want to leave the ECHR due to opinions that it destroys parliamentary sovereignty 
Tories 2019 electoral pledges to update Human rights with British Bill of Rights

HRA is an act that can be repealed with simple majority 
Judicial review is not binding on parliament

Is this a real commitment to rights or just ‘lip service’

Now in society there is a far greater awareness of ones civil liberties and thus a protection of civil rights as there is greater public support:

tables.label: Should UK parties be state funded?
rows:

State funding could be allocated based on an agreed measure of parties popularity and democratic engagement – would create level playing field for the parties and remove unfair advantages that some parties have due to wealthy donors e.g 2019 Election Tories got 12 million in party donations and Labour only got 4 million

Taxpayers may object to funding what can be considered ‘private’ organisations or parties with views that contradict their own

A reliable income stream from the state would weaken party links to the electorate and larger society – at the moment, parties need to reach out to society and recruit members and gain public trust.
